chapter: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
title: Stuff stripped in the snow, the police, and the shaking doctor
summary: Stuff wandered shirtless at ten below zero snapping his fingers; Autrey called the police, signed him into a hospital and called his sister, and a trembling doctor could not spell Smith.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Anyway, so he got -- he was walk -- coming down the street, popping his fingers (snap, snap) like he was listening to a jazz band, stripped down to his trousers, about ten below zero. Well you know that's the wrong way to be. (Laughs.) I think, and a girl was walking up the street, or down the street, whichever, and they ran into him, and he looked at her and said Hello, Baby, and kind of reached his arm out, his hand out to grab her, like he was going to brush her hair, or shoulder, something, and boy, she looked at him and saw him and she started screaming and running.

Well he didn't -- he didn't run after her. And she ran up to -- to the door, and the screen -- the door was locked, and the screen, you know, that double door, and you've got to open this, and if you're excited, man, you'll never get in.

So she was screaming, so some woman came across the street there, and say what's going on over there?! Help! I'll call the police! I say well do that, please do that. I want them myself. Call them. You know. So finally the police came and they got out, and what's going on? Say who is this? What's going on. I told them, and say oh, he says Stuff, he say you're the guys in the band down so and so. I say yeah. And he say oh, gee, I'm sorry to hear this, so they got out and they put the cuffs on him. I say I think he's all right. And he wasn't violent. He wasn't fighting, or resisting the officer, or anything. So anyway, we got through with the business. We took him to the hospital, a few miles outside of Moline there, and put him in. I had to sign for him. I had to declare him in. Naturally, under those conditions I had to sign, and signed him in, you know? And in the meantime I called his sister in Chicago, and told her what was happening, and she came down, and the next day I think she took him out and took him back to Chicago. But the doctor (laughs) the doctor who signed him in looked like he was worse than Stuff. He was shaking like, what, what, what's his name? I said Smith. How you spell, how you spell that? I say how to spell it?! Jesus Christ! (Laughter.)

How do you spell Smith? I -- you know. (Laughs.) So I looked at him, and I told him two or three times, say, what's that last name again? I say Smith. I say Smith. He say, how -- I say Smith, and he was just shaking, and putting -- changing pencils, and pens! Oh, man! This went on for about ten minutes, or more.
Well, anyway, I was glad to get out, and I didn't see Stuff anymore after that.
